--- title: "Job C — Hidden Risk" subtitle: "Tail co-crash detection: the dependence that threatens a portfolio" --- *Apply-the-tool track · Job C.* This job hunts the one kind of dependence that Pearson correlation **structurally cannot see**: the rate at which two stocks crash *together*. We climb the same ladder — a toy whose answer is beyond dispute, a stylized bank pair where we can count the co-crash by hand, then the real basket — but the **method** stays fixed throughout: a single co-crash measure, introduced once and reused unchanged as the data grows up. ("Co-crash" just means both names have a very bad day at the same time.) **What you will produce:** a tail-risk report ranking the real pairs that crash together far more often than chance would predict — the diversification illusions a trading desk would act on. --- ## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer Start where the truth is not in doubt, and recall *why* a single correlation number is the wrong tool for tail risk. `datasets.nonlinear_dependence()` draws $y = x^2 + \text{noise}$ on a symmetric range: **$y$ is (almost) fixed once you know $x$** — about as much dependence as you can have — yet the relationship is symmetric, so *Pearson must read $\approx 0$*. Pearson lies. The lesson for this job: a single number that averages over *all* values of $X$ can be blind to a dependence that only lives in one *region* of the data. Tail risk is exactly such a region — the worst days — so an averaged-over-everything correlation will miss it. ::: {#31715c97 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} x_toy: Float[Array, "n"] y_toy: Float[Array, "n"] x_toy, y_toy = datasets.nonlinear_dependence(n=1000, noise=0.05, seed=0) # y = x² + ε pear = pearsonr(x_toy, y_toy)[0] # ρ(x,y) — linear, averaged over all x spear = spearmanr(x_toy, y_toy)[0] # ρ_s(x,y) — monotone, also averaged over all x print(f"x: {x_toy.shape} y = x² + noise (y is ~determined by x)") print(f"Pearson = {pear:+.3f} (linear — reads almost nothing)") print(f"Spearman = {spear:+.3f} (monotone — also blind to the symmetry)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x: (1000,) y = x² + noise (y is ~determined by x) Pearson = +0.030 (linear — reads almost nothing) Spearman = +0.070 (monotone — also blind to the symmetry) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-toy-pearson-lies .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} left: Float[Array, "n"] = x_toy < 0 # condition on a region of x (left arm) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 5.0)) ax.scatter(x_toy[~left], y_toy[~left], s=12, c="0.78", alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none", label="right arm (x ≥ 0)") ax.scatter(x_toy[left], y_toy[left], s=14, c=WARM, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none", label="left arm (x < 0) — strongly downward") ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls="--") ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y = x² + noise") ax.set_title(f"Pearson over all x = {pear:+.2f}, yet each arm is steep", fontsize=11.5) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper center"); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Pearson lies. y = x² + noise is an almost-deterministic dependence, yet Pearson ≈ 0 because the up-arm and down-arm cancel in the average. Conditioning on a *region* of x (the left arm, shaded) reveals a strong local relationship the unconditional number erased. Tail risk lives in exactly such a region — the worst days — which is why this job conditions instead of averaging.](lab-jobC-hidden-risk_files/figure-html/fig-toy-pearson-lies-output-1.png){#fig-toy-pearson-lies width=776 height=585} ::: ::: The known answer holds: the dependence is real and strong, but every averaged-over-everything correlation reads $\approx 0$ because it cancels a region that bends one way against a region that bends the other. **The fix is to zoom in on a single region** instead of averaging over all of $X$ — and the region a portfolio fears is the tail, its worst days. That is the move the next rung turns into the co-crash measure. --- ## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market $y = x^2$ never happens in markets. What *does* happen is **joint crashes**: two banks that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones. `datasets.two_banks()` is a stylized version of that — a shared driver plus a known ~10% set of days where both names crater (the `crash_mask`). Here the answer is again known: we built the crash days ourselves, so we can count the co-crash off the mask by hand *and* check our estimate against that ground truth. **The method — zoom in on the tail.** Replace "average over all $X$" with "look only at $X$'s worst days." The co-crash fraction is a conditional probability — the chance of one event *given* that another has already happened: $$ \text{co-crash}(X, Y) \;=\; P\bigl(Y \le Q_q(Y) \,\big|\, X \le Q_q(X)\bigr) \qquad q = 0.10, $$ the chance that $Y$ is in *its* worst 10% of days, given that $X$ is in *its* worst 10% of days. A pair that moves **independently** scores $\approx q = 10\%$ — that is the baseline you compare against; a pair that crashes together scores far higher. Spelled out, with the quadrant masks made visible: ::: {#7c982f64 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def cocrash_by_hand(x: Float[Array, "n"], y: Float[Array, "n"], q: float = 0.10) -> float: """The co-crash measure, axes spelled out — P(Y in worst-q | X in worst-q). qˣ = Q_q(x), qʸ = Q_q(y) [crash lines, return units] co-crash = |{ xₜ ≤ qˣ AND yₜ ≤ qʸ }| / |{ xₜ ≤ qˣ }| """ qˣ, qʸ = np.quantile(x, q), np.quantile(y, q) # qˣ = Q_q(x), qʸ = Q_q(y) [return units] x_crash: Float[Array, "n"] = x <= qˣ # condition: X in its worst q joint: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.logical_and("n, n -> n", x_crash, y <= qʸ) # xₜ≤qˣ ∧ yₜ≤qʸ return float(joint.sum() / x_crash.sum()) # P(Y crashes | X crashes) a: Float[Array, "n"] b: Float[Array, "n"] a, b, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=1500, seed=0) print(f"{int(crash.sum())} built-in crash days of {crash.size} ({crash.mean():.0%})\n") INDEP_BASELINE = 0.10 # an independent pair scores ≈ q cc_hand = cocrash_by_hand(a, b) # our spelled-out version cc_lib = cocrash_fraction(a, b, q=0.10) # the library measure — must agree print(f"co-crash (by hand) = {cc_hand:.1%}") print(f"co-crash (library) = {cc_lib:.1%} ← same number, reused everywhere above") print(f"independence baseline= {INDEP_BASELINE:.1%}") print(f"lift over baseline = {cc_lib / INDEP_BASELINE:.1f}×") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 160 built-in crash days of 1500 (11%) co-crash (by hand) = 83.3% co-crash (library) = 83.3% ← same number, reused everywhere above independence baseline= 10.0% lift over baseline = 8.3× ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-twobanks-cocrash .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} qᵃ, qᵇ = np.quantile(a, 0.10), np.quantile(b, 0.10) # qᵃ = Q₀.₁₀(a), qᵇ = Q₀.₁₀(b) [return units] band: Float[Array, "n"] = a <= qᵃ # condition: A in its worst 10% co: Float[Array, "n"] = band & (b <= qᵇ) # aₜ≤qᵃ ∧ bₜ≤qᵇ → a co-crash hold: Float[Array, "n"] = band & (b > qᵇ) # aₜ≤qᵃ ∧ bₜ>qᵇ → B held up fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 5.2)) ax.axvspan(a.min(), qᵃ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.axhline(qᵇ, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":") ax.scatter(a[~band], b[~band], s=8, c="0.78", alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(a[hold], b[hold], s=26, c=COOL, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none", label=f"A crashes, B holds ({int(hold.sum())})") ax.scatter(a[co], b[co], s=30, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label=f"both crash — a co-crash ({int(co.sum())})") ax.text(qᵃ, ax.get_ylim()[1], " condition: A in its worst 10%", color=CRASH, fontsize=9, va="top", ha="left") ax.set_xlabel("bank A return"); ax.set_ylabel("bank B return") ax.set_title(f"Of A's {int(band.sum())} worst days, B also craters on " f"{int(co.sum())} → co-crash {cc_lib:.0%}", fontsize=11.5) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The stylized bank pair, with the co-crash quadrant shaded. The condition is the 10% of days bank A falls hardest (left band); the co-crash fraction is the share of those days on which B also breaks its crash line (red) versus shrugs it off (blue). The built-in crash days (the shared shock) pile into the lower-left corner, lifting co-crash far above the 10% independence baseline — exactly the tail an unconditional Pearson under-reads.](lab-jobC-hidden-risk_files/figure-html/fig-twobanks-cocrash-output-1.png){#fig-twobanks-cocrash width=800 height=609} ::: ::: There are two things to take away here. First, the measure is **correct**: the by-hand quadrant count and `cocrash_fraction` return the same number, and it sits far above the 10% baseline — the co-crash is real, because we built it in. Second, this is *exactly* the tail that a correlation number under-reports: Pearson averages the calm cloud and the crash corner together, while the co-crash measure keeps only the corner. We now carry this same measure, unchanged, onto the real book of stocks. --- ## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket **What we are looking for on real data:** pairs of stocks that look safely unrelated in calm times yet fall together when markets break. The co-crash number tells us, for each pair, how often the second name has one of its worst days on the same day the first name does — high means dangerous, near 10% means genuinely independent. **Receiving Tool 1's handoff.** [Tool 1's watchlist](lab-tool1-ladder.qmd) ranked real pairs by their `Pearson − Spearman` gap — a cheap, quick clue that some cross-sector pairs only move together on extreme days. The flagged names were the **diversification illusions**: utilities and energy against the rest (e.g. `CVX/DUK`, `XOM/DUK`, `GS/DUK`). Tool 1 could only *flag* them; this job runs the co-crash test that confirms the tail coupling rigorously — something no averaged-over-everything measure on that road can do. We **reload** the already-prepared returns — there is no cleaning here; the prices → log-returns pipeline and the crash-mask setting live in the data primer — display a corner of the table, and run the *same* `cocrash_fraction` from Rung 2. ::: {#2ca4d93d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() # prepared 14-name daily panel META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"])) tickers = list(R.columns) print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {len(tickers)} stocks " f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})") R[["JPM", "BAC", "GS", "XOM", "CVX", "DUK"]].iloc[:3].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4778 trading days × 14 stocks (2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

This lab reloads that panel and never re-derives the masks or the sectors. ::: First, settle Tool 1's handoff directly: run the conditional co-crash test on those exact flagged pairs, against the independence baseline. ::: {#831ea2a6 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} WATCHLIST = [("CVX", "DUK"), ("XOM", "DUK"), ("GS", "DUK")] # Tool 1's flagged pairs print("Tool 1's diversification-illusion pairs, under the conditional test:\n") print(f"{'pair':<10s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'co-crash':>10s}{'lift':>7s} sectors") print("-" * 50) for u, v in WATCHLIST: xu: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[u].values xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[v].values pe = pearsonr(xu, xv)[0] # ρ(u,v) — what Tool 1 could see cc = cocrash_fraction(xu, xv, q=0.10) # P(v crash | u crash) — conditional tail test lift = cc / INDEP_BASELINE # lift = co-crash / q print(f"{u + '/' + v:<10s}{pe:>+9.3f}{cc:>9.0%}{lift:>6.1f}×" f" {sector[u]}/{sector[v]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Tool 1's diversification-illusion pairs, under the conditional test: pair Pearson co-crash lift sectors -------------------------------------------------- CVX/DUK +0.419 30% 3.0× Energy/Utilities XOM/DUK +0.423 32% 3.2× Energy/Utilities GS/DUK +0.322 29% 2.9× Banks/Utilities ``` ::: ::: The handoff is confirmed: these cross-sector pairs have only a **modest Pearson correlation** (they look diversified in calm times) yet crash together several times more often than the 10% baseline — the tail coupling Tool 1 could flag but not measure. Now the full-basket sweep: run the same measure on every pair and assemble the co-crash matrix. ::: {#74a2517f .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import itertools rows = [] for u, v in itertools.combinations(tickers, 2): xu: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[u].values xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[v].values cc = cocrash_fraction(xu, xv, q=0.10) # P(v crash | u crash) — the Rung-2 measure, unchanged rows.append(dict(pair=f"{u}/{v}", u=u, v=v, same_sector=(sector[u] == sector[v]), pearson=pearsonr(xu, xv)[0], # ρ(u,v) cocrash=cc, lift=cc / INDEP_BASELINE)) # lift = co-crash / q rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["cocrash"], reverse=True) print(f"{len(rows)} pairs measured. strongest co-crashes:\n") print(f"{'pair':<10s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'co-crash':>10s}{'lift':>7s} sector") print("-" * 48) for r in rows[:8]: print(f"{r['pair']:<10s}{r['pearson']:>+9.3f}{r['cocrash']:>9.0%}" f"{r['lift']:>6.1f}× {'same' if r['same_sector'] else 'cross'}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 91 pairs measured. strongest co-crashes: pair Pearson co-crash lift sector ------------------------------------------------ BAC/C +0.820 72% 7.2× same XOM/CVX +0.856 70% 7.0× same JPM/BAC +0.829 70% 7.0× same JPM/C +0.763 69% 6.9× same BAC/WFC +0.825 67% 6.7× same JPM/WFC +0.823 65% 6.5× same JPM/GS +0.770 63% 6.3× same DUK/SO +0.822 63% 6.3× same ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fig-cocrash-matrix-compute .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} order = sorted(tickers, key=lambda t: (sector[t], t)) # group columns by sector n = len(order) CC: Float[Array, "n_assets n_assets"] = np.eye(n) # CC[i,j] = P(i crash | j crash); diag = 1 for i, u in enumerate(order): for j, v in enumerate(order): if i != j: xu: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[u].values xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[v].values CC[i, j] = cocrash_fraction(xv, xu, q=0.10) # P(u crash | v crash) — condition on column v secs = [sector[t] for t in order] # sector label per column bounds = [i for i in range(1, n) if secs[i] != secs[i - 1]] # indices where the sector changes ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-cocrash-matrix .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 6.4)) im = ax.imshow(CC, cmap="inferno", vmin=0.10, vmax=1.0) ax.set_xticks(range(n)); This is the conditional structure Pearson averages away.](lab-jobC-hidden-risk_files/figure-html/fig-cocrash-matrix-output-1.png){#fig-cocrash-matrix width=864 height=752} ::: ::: Read the matrix: the bank block is the obvious hot square, but the cross-sector cells away from the diagonal sit well above the 10% floor too — the market-wide drag that makes a "diversified" book fall as one. The ranking below turns this into the deliverable. --- ## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Tail-Risk Flag The deliverable is a **tail-risk report**, and it has two lists. The raw co-crash ranking is topped by the obvious same-sector pairs (the banks crash together, the energy majors crash together — everyone already knows that), so the report ranks the two groups *separately*: a within-sector list (the already-known coupling, useful for position sizing) and a **cross-sector** list — the diversification illusions. For that second group, a correlation-based risk model sets aside too little capital, because Pearson sees only the calm-time relationship and misses the joint crash. That second list is what Tool 1 handed off and what a trading desk would actually act on. ::: {#cell-fig-tailrisk-flag .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} within = [r for r in rows if r["same_sector"]][:8] # known coupling — for sizing cross = [r for r in rows if not r["same_sector"]][:8] # the diversification illusions for title, queue in [("within-sector (known coupling)", within), ("cross-sector (diversification illusions → act on these)", cross)]: print(f"\n{title}\n{'pair':<10s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'co-crash':>10s}{'lift':>7s}") print("-" * 36) for r in queue: print(f"{r['pair']:<10s}{r['pearson']:>+9.3f}{r['cocrash']:>9.0%}{r['lift']:>6.1f}×") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8, 4.6)) queue = within[::-1] + cross[::-1] # barh: within fills the bottom, cross the top colors = [COOL] * len(within) + [CRASH] * len(cross) ax.barh([r["pair"] for r in queue], [100 * r["cocrash"] for r in queue], color=colors) ax.axvline(100 * INDEP_BASELINE, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independence baseline (10%)") ax.axhline(len(within) - 0.5, color=INK, lw=0.8) # divider between the two queues ax.text(0.99, len(within) - 0.5, "within-sector ", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9, color=COOL, fontweight="bold") ax.text(0.99, len(within) + len(cross) - 0.5, "cross-sector ", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold") ax.set_xlabel("co-crash (% of one name's worst days the other also crashes)") ax.set_title("Tail-risk flag — two queues a desk reads differently", fontsize=12) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right") despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` within-sector (known coupling) pair Pearson co-crash lift ------------------------------------ BAC/C +0.820 72% 7.2× XOM/CVX +0.856 70% 7.0× JPM/BAC +0.829 70% 7.0× JPM/C +0.763 69% 6.9× BAC/WFC +0.825 67% 6.7× JPM/WFC +0.823 65% 6.5× JPM/GS +0.770 63% 6.3× DUK/SO +0.822 63% 6.3× cross-sector (diversification illusions → act on these) pair Pearson co-crash lift ------------------------------------ C/CVX +0.482 46% 4.6× JPM/CVX +0.525 46% 4.6× BAC/CVX +0.486 45% 4.5× GS/CVX +0.537 45% 4.5× WFC/CVX +0.488 44% 4.4× GS/MSFT +0.486 44% 4.4× JPM/MSFT +0.455 42% 4.2× JPM/XOM +0.491 42% 4.2× ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The tail-risk flag, split into the two queues a desk reads differently. These are the pairs Tool 1 flagged and a covariance-based risk model under-reserves.](lab-jobC-hidden-risk_files/figure-html/fig-tailrisk-flag-output-2.png){#fig-tailrisk-flag width=920 height=537} ::: ::: Read the cross-sector list as the triage queue: these are the pairs whose joint crashes a covariance matrix most badly understates, by counting them as a diversification benefit that is not really there. They look diversified to Pearson and are not, in the only situation that matters — the bad days — and they crash together two to three times more often than the baseline despite modest correlation, exactly the illusion Tool 1 flagged and this test confirms. --- ## How Deep Is the Illusion? Sweep the Tail The co-crash setting `q` controls how bad a day has to be to count as a "crash" — a smaller `q` means a deeper, rarer loss. The diversification illusion is not fixed: it gets **worse** the further into the tail you look. Sweep `q` for the flagged cross-sector pairs: ::: {#7b9c1bb4 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"{'pair':<10s}{'q=20%':>8s}{'q=10%':>8s}{'q=5%':>8s} (co-crash lift over baseline)") for pair in ["CVX/DUK", "XOM/DUK", "GS/DUK"]: a, b = pair.split("/") x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[a].to_numpy() y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[b].to_numpy() lift = [cocrash_fraction(x, y, q=q) / q for q in (0.20, 0.10, 0.05)] # lift = P(y crash|x crash) / q print(f"{pair:<10s}{lift[0]:>7.1f}x{lift[1]:>7.1f}x{lift[2]:>7.1f}x") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pair q=20% q=10% q=5% (co-crash lift over baseline) CVX/DUK 1.8x 3.0x 5.9x XOM/DUK 1.9x 3.2x 5.8x GS/DUK 1.7x 2.9x 5.5x ``` ::: ::: The pattern is the warning. At a mild 20% threshold these pairs crash together under twice as often as the baseline — easy to wave away — but zoom in on the *worst 5%* of days and that multiple roughly triples, to about 6×. The tail dependence a covariance matrix misses is worst exactly where it hurts most: in the deepest losses. This is the flag a desk acts on, and the reason the [uncertainty](../../uncertainty/index.qmd) chapter refuses to model the joint tail with a Gaussian, and the [gaussianization](../../gaussianization/index.qmd) chapter learns the true joint shape instead.
